The Blackfin sucker, Thoburnia atripinnis, a benthic catostomid endemic to upland streams of the Cumberland Plateau, reaches an ultimate total length of approximately 17 centimeters [Li = approximately 17 centimeters]. As a relatively small-bodied member of its genus, this species occupies cool, well-oxygenated riffles where it feeds predominantly on benthic macroinvertebrates. Field surveys conducted over several years indicate that males and females both achieve this maximum size, though growth rates vary considerably among drainages. Individual growth trajectories appear strongly influenced by local thermal regimes and food availability, with populations in colder headwaters typically attaining smaller asymptotic sizes. Analysis of scale annuli from older specimens reveals that most individuals require several growing seasons to approach this upper limit. In comparison to the larger-bodied redhorse suckers of the genus Moxostoma, the Blackfin sucker's modest ultimate length reflects its restriction to smaller stream habitats where space and trophic resources are more constrained. The total length at which this species reaches puberty is 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters], a size typically achieved near the end of the third growing season for most individuals. This length marks the onset of gonadal development and vitellogenesis in females, at which point they are approximately one-half of their maximum possible length.

Neonatal individuals of Thoburnia atripinnis emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs that are deposited over gravel substrates. Upon hatching, the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on its endogenous reserves before beginning exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0082 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0082 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of roughly 2.5 millimeters, which yields a spherical volume that translates to this modest initial mass. This minute birth mass is consistent with the pattern seen in other small-bodied catostomids, where high fecundity is balanced by minimal per-offspring investment. The newly emerged prolarvae remain hidden within the interstitial spaces of the gravel bed for several days, absorbing yolk material and undergoing early organogenesis. By the time the mouth opens and the yolk sac is fully resorbed, the small larvae must locate suitable prey items such as microcrustaceans and chironomid larvae. During this period, mortality rates are exceedingly high, a natural consequence of the low birth mass and the intense predation pressure exerted by crayfish and other riffle-dwelling predators. Endotrophic larvae that survive to the onset of feeding begin a rapid phase of somatic growth that carries them through the summer months.

Reproductive output in Thoburnia atripinnis is notably high relative to its body size. Gravid females produce between 1 and 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 1 and 3 eggs per clutch], and spawning activity is concentrated during a brief period in early spring when water temperatures reach approximately 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. Within that thermal window, females deposit roughly 1 clutch per day [F_R_i = roughly 1 clutch per day] over a span of several days, resulting in a substantial total seasonal fecundity. A typical adult female measuring 16.8 centimeters in total length and 14.6 centimeters in standard length can release hundreds of eggs over the course of the spawning season. This reproductive strategy, characterized by small clutch sizes produced at a high daily frequency, resembles the pattern documented in the greater redhorse, Moxostoma valenciennesi, whose similar fecundity schedule informed the estimates for this species. Interannual variation in stream flow and temperature influences the exact timing and intensity of the spawning bout; years with prolonged cold snaps can delay the onset of gamete release. Males arrive on the spawning grounds first, establishing territories in shallow riffles where they await ripe females.

The wet weight at puberty, corresponding to the 8 centimeter length at which gonadal recrudescence begins, is approximately 5.56 grams [Wwp = approximately 5.56 grams]. This mass marks the transition from the juvenile growth phase into the reproductive stage of the life cycle. By contrast, the ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adults is approximately 55 grams [Wwi = approximately 55 grams], a value consistent with the length-weight relationship derived from the species' allometric growth coefficient. The threefold increase in mass between puberty and adulthood reflects the continued somatic investment that occurs even after the onset of reproductive activity. In many female Blackfin suckers, the post-puberty growth period is critical for accumulating the lipid reserves necessary to fuel successive annual spawning bouts. Fish that attain a larger adult mass tend to produce more clutches per season and enjoy higher overall fecundity. This correlation between body mass and reproductive output is common among iteroparous stream fishes, where larger body size confers a competitive advantage in accessing prime spawning territories and in resisting periods of low food availability. Field data from a long-term study on the Cumberland Plateau confirm that females exceeding 45 grams are the most prolific members of the population.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Thoburnia atripinnis under natural stream conditions reaches 4 years [am = 4 years], with the oldest individuals documented in populations occupying stable, thermally buffered spring-fed streams at an average water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This relatively short longevity is typical for small-bodied catostomids inhabiting dynamic lotic environments where periodic flood events and high metabolic costs accelerate senescence. Age determination from otolith microstructure confirms that very few individuals survive beyond their fourth winter, as accumulated physiological wear from repeated spawning events and the energetic demands of living in cool, fast-flowing water take a cumulative toll. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the Blackfin sucker's lifespan is near the lower end of the range for the tribe Catostomini. In warmer, more productive streams, growth rates are faster but longevity appears to be somewhat reduced, possibly due to elevated metabolic rates associated with higher ambient temperatures. The 4-year lifespan imposes strong selective pressure for early maturation and high reproductive investment in the first few spawning seasons, a life-history syndrome that aligns with the relatively small size at puberty and the high daily egg production rate observed in this species.
